summary: Defines a :copy keyword parameter for the Sieve mail filtering language, letting fileinto and redirect actions deliver a copy without cancelling the default save to the inbox. Users get filing or forwarding without losing the original.

plainLanguage.summary: Normally, when a mail rule moves a letter, it leaves the inbox. This addition lets the rule make a copy so the original stays.

questions: sieve fileinto without cancelling implicit keep
what is the sieve copy extension
how to copy a message with sieve fileinto
sieve redirect without cancelling inbox delivery
subtitle: A Sieve ':copy' option that files or forwards an extra copy of a message without cancelling normal delivery.

tldr.problem: In Sieve, 'fileinto' and 'redirect' cancel the default save to the inbox, so keeping an extra copy needs awkward explicit 'keep' commands that interact badly with later rules.
tldr.mechanism: The ':copy' parameter on 'fileinto' and 'redirect' files or redirects a copy in addition to whatever else happens to the message, leaving the implicit keep in place.
tldr.outcome: Users and tools can add copying commands to a script without changing the meaning of the rest of it, but the feature makes quiet eavesdropping on mail easier.

today: RFC 3894 is a Proposed Standard and the metadata lists no RFC that obsoletes or updates it.

sections.title: The Problem with Explicit Keep
sections.content:
The Sieve language lets users control how incoming e-mail is handled. By default a message is saved in the owner's inbox, and actions such as fileinto and redirect cancel that default.

A user who only wants an extra copy could write fileinto "unfiltered"; keep;. But the explicit keep is a poor substitute for the implicit one when more processing follows: a later discard is ineffective against it, so a discarded message still ends up in the inbox.

Perfectly expressive Sieve code is possible, but it quickly grows unwieldy because it must track the state the implicit keep would have had.
sections.plainLanguage: If you tell a helper to 'also keep it' and then later 'throw away junk', the helper keeps the junk anyway. A copy option avoids that mix-up.

sections.title: The :copy Parameter
sections.content:
The extension adds an optional :copy keyword to two commands: fileinto [":copy"] <folder: string> and redirect [":copy"] <address: string>. With it, the command does not cancel the implicit keep; it merely files or redirects a copy in addition to whatever else is happening to the message.

The capability string is copy, so a script says require ["copy", "fileinto"]; before using it. The RFC's example is fileinto :copy "incoming";.
sections.plainLanguage: Adding the word 'copy' tells the rule: make a duplicate, and leave the original where it was.

sections.title: Eavesdropping Risk
sections.content:
The extension makes it easier to eavesdrop on a user's message stream without the user noticing. This was technically possible before for an attacker with read/write access to a user's Sieve scripts, but now the attacker no longer needs to parse a script to modify it.

Write access to Sieve scripts must therefore be protected as strongly as read/write access to e-mail. The RFC also tells organizations that monitor mail to learn local data protection laws and to set users' privacy expectations correctly.
sections.plainLanguage: Because making secret copies got easier, the keys to your rules must be guarded as carefully as your mailbox.

sections.title: IANA Registration
sections.content: The RFC registers the Sieve extension with capability name copy, capability keyword copy and no capability arguments, with RFC 3894 as the Standards Track reference.
sections.plainLanguage: The new word was written down in an official list so everyone spells it the same way.

references.text: Showalter, T., "Sieve: A Mail Filtering Language", RFC 3028, January 2001.
